The first man, and lord of the dead
A class of fire-priest — the name behind the Atharvaveda

blocks.html: This is not a list of resemblances. It is a systematic correspondence covering the language, the pantheon, the priesthood, the ritual and the ethical vocabulary — which means the Vedic and the Zoroastrian traditions are two branches of one thing, separated somewhere and drifting apart. Notably, some terms invert: daēva, cognate with Vedic deva, means demon in Avestan, while ahura means God — a mirror-image of the later Indian situation. Older scholarship read this as evidence of a religious schism; most specialists now treat the causes as unresolved. The correspondence itself is not in doubt by anyone.
The Letter from Anatolia
And then there is the piece of evidence that comes with an external date attached, which is why it matters so much.

In the second millennium BCE there was a kingdom called Mitanni in northern Syria and northern Iraq. Its population spoke Hurrian, a language unrelated to Sanskrit. But its ruling elite bore names, and worshipped gods, and used technical terms, that are unmistakably Indo-Aryan.

items: A treaty between the Hittite king Šuppiluliuma and the Mitanni ruler Šattiwaza, recovered from the Hittite archives at Boğazköy and dated to around 1380 BCE, calls upon a list of divine witnesses that includes — in cuneiform, in a Hurrian-language document, in Syria — Mitra, Varuṇa, Indra and the Nāsatyas. Four gods of the Rigveda, invoked as a group, in a dated diplomatic document a very long way from the Punjab.

A manual on the training of chariot horses, written by a Mitanni horse-master named Kikkuli, uses technical numerals for the number of laps: aika-, tera-, panza-, satta-, na- — one, three, five, seven, nine. Compare Sanskrit eka, tri, pañca, sapta, nava.

That first numeral is doing decisive work. Aika corresponds to Sanskrit eka, "one" — and specifically not to the Iranian form aiva. The Mitanni terms are therefore Indo-Aryan rather than Iranian, meaning the two branches had already separated before this material reached Syria.

blocks.html: So by about 1380 BCE — a date fixed by Near Eastern chronology, which is independent of anything Indian — Indo-Aryan gods with recognisably Vedic names and a specialised Indo-Aryan chariot vocabulary were present among an elite in Syria. This is the hardest external anchor the subject has.
A Timeline

items.html: The reconstructed ancestral language of a family stretching from Ireland to Bengal. The mainstream position places its homeland in the Pontic–Caspian steppe. Its reconstructed vocabulary includes wheel, axle and yoke — so the language cannot be much older than wheeled transport.
Great cities at Mohenjo-daro, Harappa, Dholavira and Rakhigarhi; standardised weights, drainage, seals, long-distance trade. Its script is undeciphered, so its language is unknown.

items.what: Sintashta and Andronovo, Central Asian steppe
items.html: Cultures associated with the Indo-Iranian branch. Sintashta burials contain the earliest known spoked-wheel chariots, with horse sacrifice and a ritual repertoire resembling what the Vedic and Avestan texts describe.

Urban centres shrink or are abandoned; population shifts eastward and to smaller settlements. Explanations centre on hydrological and monsoon change and disrupted trade. There is no destruction horizon attributable to invaders.

items.what: The Bactria–Margiana complex, and movement south
items.html: Indo-Iranian speakers move south through Central Asia, interacting with the settled BMAC cultures — a region from which Vedic Sanskrit is argued to have picked up a layer of non-Indo-European loanwords.

The family books, in the region of the Sapta Sindhu — the seven rivers of the greater Punjab. This is the conventional range and the one most specialists use. It is a range, not a date, and its edges are soft.
Mitra, Varuṇa, Indra and the Nāsatyas invoked in a Hittite–Mitanni treaty in Anatolia. Externally dated.

items.what: Books 1, 9 and 10; the collection is arranged
items.html: The latest maṇḍalas — including the Nāsadīya and the Puruṣa Sūkta — are composed, and the Rigveda is fixed in the order we have it.

The Yajurveda, Samaveda and Atharvaveda Samhitas take shape. Iron comes into use, rice becomes central, and the geography of the texts shifts to the Ganga–Yamuna region. The Kuru realm consolidates, and is argued to be where the corpus was first systematically organised.
The great ritual prose, including the Śatapatha. The śrauta system reaches its full elaboration; the Śulbasūtra geometry develops alongside it.
Bṛhadāraṇyaka and Chāndogya, then the others. The corpus turns inward. The Buddha and Mahāvīra arrive within a century or two, into an intellectual world these texts had already opened.
The Aṣṭādhyāyī fixes the description of the language. Yāska's Nirukta, roughly of this era, shows that the Rigveda already required a glossary.

items.what: Writing is abundant — and the Veda stays oral
items.html: The Ashokan inscriptions show literacy in routine administration. The Vedic corpus goes on being transmitted by mouth for centuries more, by deliberate policy.

items.what: Sāyaṇa, and the oldest surviving manuscripts
items.html: Sāyaṇa, under Vijayanagara patronage, produces the commentary on the Rigveda that remains standard. The earliest Rigveda manuscripts we possess date from around this period.

items.what: Sir William Jones names the family
items.html: In an address to the Asiatic Society in Calcutta, Jones observes that Sanskrit bears to Greek and Latin "a stronger affinity… than could possibly have been produced by accident," and proposes a common source. Comparative Indo-European linguistics begins here.
Max Müller publishes the first complete edition with Sāyaṇa's commentary, in six volumes. For the first time the text can be read by anyone who can read Sanskrit.
Excavation reveals a Bronze Age urban civilisation nobody had suspected — and creates the question that has occupied the field ever since: what, if anything, connects those cities to these hymns?

Narasimhan and colleagues publish a large ancient-genome study in Science, adding an independent line of evidence to a question argued for two centuries on linguistic and archaeological grounds alone.

blocks.html: The Origins Question

Now the part of this subject that generates more heat than all the rest of it combined. I am going to set it out carefully, state the mainstream position and its evidence, state the dissenting position and its main claims fairly, and then say honestly why most specialists do not accept the dissent. I am not going to be rude about anybody, and I am going to be clear about what the evidence does and does not establish — including where it establishes considerably less than partisans on either side would like.
The mainstream position, stated precisely

The Indo-Aryan languages arrived in South Asia from outside it, most probably via Central Asia, in the second millennium BCE. The Indo-Aryan branch descends from Indo-Iranian, which descends from Proto-Indo-European, whose speakers are generally located in the Pontic–Caspian steppe. The evidence is of three kinds:

items: Comparative linguistics. Sanskrit is one branch of a family with roughly ten other branches — Iranian, Greek, Italic, Celtic, Germanic, Balto-Slavic, Armenian, Anatolian, Tocharian, Albanian — every one of which is located outside South Asia. The standard principle for locating a language family's origin is that it lies where the deepest diversity is, and the diversity is not in India. The reconstructed proto-vocabulary contains terms for the wheel, the axle and wool, which dates the parent language to after these things existed. And Vedic Sanskrit itself contains a layer of loanwords from non-Indo-European sources, along with features such as retroflex consonants that are typical of South Asia and unusual in the wider family — the signature of an incoming language absorbing what it met.

Archaeology. The Sintashta–Andronovo horizon of the Central Asian steppe shows chariots, horses, and burial and sacrificial practices that correspond closely to what the Vedic and Avestan texts describe, in the right period, in a position from which movement south is straightforward.

Ancient DNA. The 2019 Science paper led by Vagheesh Narasimhan, analysing hundreds of ancient genomes from Central and South Asia, found that steppe-pastoralist-related ancestry entered South Asia in the second millennium BCE. Individuals associated with the Indus civilisation lacked it. Modern South Asian populations are modelled as mixtures that include it. A companion study of an individual from Rakhigarhi, published the same year, was consistent with that picture.

blocks.tag: Historical Lens · What This Is Not

blocks.html: This must be said with complete clarity, because it is the point on which the whole conversation goes wrong. The evidence is about language and ancestry. It is not evidence of an invasion.

The "Aryan invasion" — chariot-borne warriors sweeping in and destroying the Indus cities — is a nineteenth- and early-twentieth-century construction, and the evidence does not support it. There is no destruction layer at Indus sites attributable to incomers. Mortimer Wheeler's mid-century reading of unburied skeletons at Mohenjo-daro as massacre victims — his phrase was that "Indra stands accused" — was reexamined by later specialists, notably by the biological anthropologist Kenneth Kennedy, and does not survive: the skeletons are not from a single event, do not show a pattern of battle trauma, and do not date to the relevant moment. The Indus decline substantially predates the period in question and is now attributed chiefly to environmental and economic causes.

The framing also carried nineteenth-century racial theory inside it, and was later put to appalling use in Europe. The word ārya in the Vedic texts is a self-designation meaning something like "noble" or "one of us" — a cultural and linguistic term, not a racial one, and not a designation of a biological population.

What the evidence supports is migration: mobile pastoralist populations moving south over generations, in numbers sufficient to leave a genetic trace and to transmit a language, into a region that was already populous and had its own long civilisation. Language shift of this kind — a language spreading without population replacement or material rupture — is one of the best-documented processes in history. Latin, Arabic and Turkish all did it.
The indigenous-origin position, stated fairly

There is a body of work, produced by serious people, arguing that Indo-Aryan speakers were indigenous to South Asia, that the Vedic culture is the Indus civilisation or its direct heir, and in its stronger form that Indo-European languages spread outward from India. It is associated with, among others, the archaeologist B. B. Lal in his later work, and with writers including Shrikant Talageri, Koenraad Elst and Michel Danino. Its principal arguments are these.

items: The Sarasvatī argument. The Rigveda praises the Sarasvatī as a mighty river running from the mountains to the sea — nadītamā, greatest of rivers — and Rigveda 10.75 lists it in a sequence of rivers between the Yamunā and the Sutudrī (Sutlej), which points to the bed of the Ghaggar–Hakra. That river system dried up. If hymns describe it as mighty, the argument runs, they must have been composed while it was mighty — which pushes the Rigveda back before the drying, and therefore into or before the Harappan period, and therefore rules out an arrival in the second millennium.

The continuity argument. Archaeology shows no rupture: pottery traditions, settlement patterns and craft techniques develop continuously through the second millennium in northwest India. Skeletal studies, including Kennedy's, found no evidence of a population discontinuity at the relevant period. If a new population arrived, where is it in the ground?

The absence-of-memory argument. The Rigveda's geography is Indian. It knows the Sapta Sindhu, the Punjab rivers, the Sarasvatī. It contains no narrative of migration from elsewhere, no memory of a homeland left behind, no account of arrival.
Astronomical dating. Readings of astronomical references in Vedic texts as records of precession, yielding dates far earlier than the linguistic consensus.

The colonial-provenance argument. The migration model was formulated by European scholars during colonial rule, in an intellectual climate saturated with racial theory, and served a narrative in which Indian civilisation's achievements were credited to outsiders. This argument is about the origins of a theory rather than its truth, but the historical observation behind it is accurate and should not be waved away.

blocks.html: Why most linguists and geneticists do not accept it
Here are the reasons, stated as reasons rather than as dismissals.

items: The linguistic problem is the heavy one, and it is structural. An Indian homeland requires that every other branch of the family — Celtic, Germanic, Italic, Greek, Balto-Slavic, Anatolian, Tocharian and the rest — departed India, while Indo-Aryan alone remained, and that the whole family's diversity accumulated after departure. It also requires explaining why Indo-Aryan shares a specific set of innovations exclusively with Iranian, which is exactly what you expect if the two separated recently and near each other, and hard to arrange from an Indian centre. No proposal has yet accounted for the distribution of the family under an Indian homeland in a way that has persuaded working comparative linguists.

The chronological problem. The reconstructed parent language contains wheeled-vehicle vocabulary shared across the family, which places it after the mid-fourth millennium BCE. An Indian homeland old enough to precede the Indus civilisation is too early for the language the method reconstructs.

The substrate problem. Vedic Sanskrit contains non-Indo-European vocabulary — plant names, agricultural terms, place names — and the proportion increases as the corpus proceeds. That pattern is what a language arriving in an inhabited region looks like. It is difficult to explain in a language that had always been where it was.

The Mitanni problem. Indo-Aryan names, gods and chariot terms appear in Syria around 1380 BCE, in a form already distinct from Iranian. Under the mainstream model this is a branch that separated on the way south and turned west. Under an out-of-India model it requires a separate long-distance migration from India to Syria for which there is no other evidence.

The genetic evidence now constrains the question directly. Steppe-related ancestry appears in South Asia in the second millennium BCE and is absent from the Indus-associated individuals so far sampled. This does not, by itself, prove which language anybody spoke — genetics tracks people, not words, and the distinction genuinely matters. But it establishes that a population movement of the right kind happened at the right time, which removes the objection that no such movement is detectable.

blocks.html: And the crucial methodological point, which cuts across the whole argument: the continuity evidence is real and does not establish what it is offered to establish. The absence of an invasion is not the presence of indigenous origin. Migration accompanied by language shift, without destruction, without population replacement, and without a break in pottery styles, is the normal case rather than the exception. Both sides of this debate have at times argued as though disproving the invasion settles the question. It does not, because the mainstream position stopped claiming an invasion decades ago.

blocks.tag: Reflect · On Why This Is Not a Neutral Argument

blocks.html: It is worth being honest about why this particular question is so charged, because pretending it is a purely technical dispute helps nobody. For a great many Indians, the migration model arrived attached to a colonial claim that everything valuable in Indian civilisation came from outside, and that claim was made by people with power over them. That memory is real, the grievance behind it has a factual basis, and someone who resists the model for that reason is not being irrational; they are declining to trust a source that earned distrust.

The reply is not contempt. It is that the model has changed in exactly the direction the objection demanded — the invasion is gone, the racial framing is gone, the Indus civilisation is understood as a great achievement in its own right and not a prelude to anything — while the linguistic core has been repeatedly tested and has held. And there is a further point that deserves stating plainly: nothing about the Vedas' value depends on the answer. The hymns are exactly as old, as beautiful and as extraordinarily preserved either way. A tradition that has been secure for three thousand years does not need this argument to come out one way.
The Three Lenses on One Question

items.title: Scriptural
items.html: The Veda is apauruṣeya — without human author, without beginning. The ṛṣis did not compose the hymns; they saw them. The Mīmāṁsā school argued the Veda's eternity as a philosophical position, holding that the relation between word and meaning is itself beginningless. On this account the question "when was it written" is a category error.

items.title: Symbolic
items.html: The claim of authorlessness does real work regardless of chronology: it says the truth of the Veda does not rest on anyone's authority, credentials or era. Nothing is true here because a great man said it. What is heard is prior to the hearer. Read that way, apauruṣeya is a statement about the nature of the transmission, not a dating claim in competition with the historians.

items.title: Historical
items.html: Composed by identifiable families of poets, in a datable form of an Indo-European language, in a period most specialists place around 1500–1200 BCE for the oldest core, with later material extending several centuries on. The tightest external anchor is a Hittite treaty of about 1380 BCE. Every part of this is revisable if the evidence changes.

blocks.html: These do not need to be reconciled and should not be. They are answers to different questions, and the discipline of keeping them apart is what makes it possible to hold all three at once — which is, in the end, the only intellectually honest position available to someone who both loves this material and wants to know what is true about it.

sections.label: Chapter 09 · Evidence
sections.title: What Science Actually Says
sections.subtitle: The claims made about the Vedas, tested honestly — corroborated, open, and contradicted

blocks.html: Every course in this library ends here, and if you read one chapter of this one, let it be this. For eight chapters we have been inside the material — what the hymns say, how they were kept, where they came from. Now we step outside and ask a different question in a different voice: what can actually be shown? Not what is beautiful. Not what is meaningful. What survives contact with evidence.

The Vedas attract more false claims than any other body of ancient literature, and they attract them from both directions. One side inflates: the hymns encode the speed of light, the law of gravitation, the age of the universe, aircraft, nuclear weapons. The other side deflates: it is primitive fire-worship and nothing more, of antiquarian interest only. These look like opposites. They are the same error — both assume that unless a text is a physics paper, it is worthless. Neither camp has read very much of it.
The Rules I Am Working Under

items: Name the finding. "Scientists have proven" is a rumour about evidence, not evidence. Where a specific study exists you get the researchers, the venue and roughly when. Where I can only describe the state of a field, I say so, and I invent nothing.
"No evidence for" is not "evidence against." Collapsing these is the commonest dishonesty in this territory, and it is committed as often by sceptics as by enthusiasts.
A tradition can be extraordinary without being right. The oral transmission is genuinely one of the great achievements of the human species. That fact has no bearing on whether Indra exists.

Nothing here needs to win. If a claim fails, it fails. The Rigveda is not diminished by the universe being 13.8 billion years old, and the people who feel it is have misunderstood what kind of thing they are defending.

blocks.html: The Verdicts

items.claim: The Vedas have been transmitted orally, with extraordinary fidelity, for roughly three thousand years.
items.html: Documented, examinable, and astonishing. The Vedic schools built layered redundancy into the act of recitation: the word-by-word pada text, the overlapping krama, and the permuted jaṭā and ghana formats in which every word is recited many times in forward and reverse order — reversal deliberately removing the crutch of meaning. Strict metre supplies a syllable-count check; the preserved pitch accent supplies another. A corruption must satisfy all of these simultaneously to survive, which is the structure of an error-detecting code. Recitation traditions separated for centuries agree to a degree that textual critics do not encounter elsewhere in antiquity, and the accent has been preserved for two thousand years after it ceased to exist in spoken language — closely enough that it corresponds to the accent independently reconstructed for Proto-Indo-European from ancient Greek. UNESCO proclaimed the tradition of Vedic chanting a Masterpiece of Oral and Intangible Heritage in 2003 and inscribed it on the Representative List in 2008. And the exact limit must be stated: this establishes that the words are old and nearly unchanged. It establishes nothing whatsoever about whether what the words say is true. Fidelity is a property of copying, not of content.

items.claim: The language of the Rigveda is genuinely archaic — among the oldest substantial texts in any Indo-European language.
items.html: This is not a matter of tradition or assertion; it is established by ordinary historical linguistics. Rigvedic Sanskrit preserves grammatical categories that Classical Sanskrit lost — the subjunctive, a far richer infinitival system, a functioning pitch accent — and its internal strata can be ordered by language alone, with the family books (maṇḍalas 2–7) demonstrably older than books 1, 9 and 10. Its content matches: the text knows the horse and the spoked-wheel chariot, does not know iron, and does not know rice, all of which are datable. The conventional range of roughly 1500–1200 BCE for the oldest core is well supported. What will never be supported is precision: anyone offering you a year is selling something.

items.claim: The Vedic and Iranian traditions are two branches of one ancestral religion, and Indo-Aryan gods are attested in Syria by about 1380 BCE.
items.html: The Avestan parallel is exact and systematic rather than impressionistic: a regular sound correspondence converts Vedic s to Avestan h, and applying it yields soma/haoma, yajña/yasna, hotṛ/zaotar, ṛta/aša, asura/ahura, Mitra/Mithra, Yama/Yima — language, pantheon, priesthood, ritual and ethics all corresponding at once. The Anatolian evidence adds an externally dated anchor: a Hittite–Mitanni treaty from the archives at Boğazköy, around 1380 BCE, invokes Mitra, Varuṇa, Indra and the Nāsatyas as divine witnesses, and the Mitanni horse-training manual of Kikkuli uses Indo-Aryan numerals, with aika ("one") matching Sanskrit eka rather than the Iranian form. This is as solid as anything in the subject.

items.claim: Vedic ritual generated real and early achievements in geometry, phonetics and grammar.
items.html: The Śulbasūtras — altar-construction manuals attached to the ritual literature, attributed to Baudhāyana, Āpastamba, Kātyāyana and Mānava and generally dated to somewhere around the eighth to sixth centuries BCE — state the relation between a rectangle's diagonal and its sides that Europe names after Pythagoras, give procedures for transforming one shape into another of equal area, and give a good approximation for the square root of two. They are stated as construction rules rather than as proved theorems, which is a real difference from the Greek tradition and not a defect to be argued away. The phonetic analysis in the Prātiśākhya literature, and Pāṇini's grammar of around the fourth century BCE, are of a technical order that twentieth-century linguists found startling; Leonard Bloomfield called the Aṣṭādhyāyī one of the greatest monuments of human intelligence. These are the genuine scientific achievements of this tradition, and they are ignored by exactly the people who claim it contains modern physics.

items.claim: Soma can be identified with a particular plant.
items.html: Genuinely unresolved, and it is a live research question rather than a dead one. The hymns constrain the answer — pressed stalks, crushed between stones, drunk immediately without fermentation, tawny in colour, from mountains, powerfully stimulating, and notably not described as producing visions. Ephedra fits best on most counts, and decisively so on one: the Iranian branch of the same tradition uses ephedra for haoma, the same word and the same rite. Amanita muscaria, argued at book length by R. Gordon Wasson in Soma: Divine Mushroom of Immortality (1968), fits the pressed-stalk description badly and the geography worse, and rests partly on a reading of one verse as describing the ritual drinking of urine, which most Vedicists do not accept. Syrian rue, argued by David Flattery and Martin Schwartz in Haoma and Harmaline (1989), has the same plant-part problem. Archaeologically, Viktor Sarianidi reported residues he identified as ephedra at Bronze Age ritual sites in Turkmenistan; later analyses by other researchers questioned those identifications. The tradition itself lost the plant: ritual manuals discuss substitutes, and the fire rituals performed today use a creeper with no intoxicating effect at all.

items.claim: The Rigvedic Sarasvatī is the Ghaggar–Hakra, and the hymns describing it as mighty must predate its drying.
items.html: This is contested among specialists and I am not going to pretend otherwise. For: the Rigveda calls the Sarasvatī the greatest of rivers, flowing from mountain to sea, and Rigveda 10.75 places it between the Yamunā and the Sutlej, which points squarely at the Ghaggar–Hakra bed; a large number of Harappan-era sites lie along that system. Against: palaeohydrological work has complicated the picture considerably — a 2017 study in Nature Communications argued that the Ghaggar–Hakra was not a glacier-fed Himalayan river during the period of Harappan urbanism, the major Himalayan feeder having shifted away millennia earlier, which would mean a monsoon-fed seasonal system rather than a mighty stream at the relevant time. There is also a further complication that cuts both ways: Sarasvatī corresponds to Avestan Haraxvaitī, a river name in the Iranian world, and river names travel with the people who use them. And the inference is weaker than it looks even if the identification holds: hymns can praise a river in inherited formulaic language long after it has diminished, and a mighty Sarasvatī would establish a date for particular verses, not for the corpus. Unresolved, and worth watching — this is one of the places where new evidence could genuinely move the field.

items.claim: Astronomical references in Vedic texts can date them precisely — some say to 4500 BCE or earlier.
items.html: The method is real and the results are not reliable, and it is worth understanding exactly why. B. G. Tilak, in The Orion (1893) and The Arctic Home in the Vedas (1903), read references to the position of the equinox against the constellations as datable observations, and used the precession of the equinoxes — a genuine 26,000-year cycle — to assign very early dates. Later workers have attempted similar readings, often centring on the statement in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa about the Kṛttikās (the Pleiades) rising due east. The difficulty is that the calculation is extremely sensitive to assumptions that the texts do not supply: which star or asterism a name denotes, whether a statement is an observation or a schematic convention inherited unchanged, what degree of precision an unaided naked-eye observer could achieve, and whether a phrase is even astronomical rather than ritual. Vary any of these within defensible limits and the resulting date moves by many centuries — sometimes by millennia. This is not a claim that the early dates are false; it is that the method cannot discriminate between them and the conventional dates, and a technique that returns whatever you assume is not evidence. Note also that these dates conflict with the linguistic and archaeological evidence, and no astronomical argument has yet been made that specialists in those fields have found compelling.

items.claim: The Vedas record the speed of light.
items.html: This is the most widely circulated of all the claims, and it does not survive contact with the actual text. The claim rests on a line in Sāyaṇa's commentary on Rigveda 1.50.4, which quotes a remembered verse: yojanānāṁ sahasre dve dve śate dve ca yojane | ekena nimiṣārdhena kramamāṇa namo'stu te — "salutations to you who traverse 2,202 yojanas in half a nimeṣa." Choose a yojana of about nine miles and a nimeṣa of about 16/75 of a second and the arithmetic gives roughly 186,000 miles per second. Every step of the argument fails. (1) It is not in the Vedas. Sāyaṇa wrote in the fourteenth century CE, some two and a half thousand years after the hymn, and he explicitly presents the line as a quotation from elsewhere. (2) The verse is addressed to the sun and describes the sun's own travel — kramamāṇa, "O you who stride" — not the propagation of light. (3) The units are not fixed. Indian sources give the yojana wildly varying values, commonly anywhere from about four to about nine miles or more, and the nimeṣa likewise; the match is manufactured by selecting the values that produce it, and other equally defensible values are off by a factor of two or more. (4) The actual verse being commented on says nothing of the sort — Rigveda 1.50.4 reads taraṇir viśvadarśato jyotiṣkṛd asi sūrya, "swift and all-seen are you, maker of light, O Sun." (5) And decisively: there is no accompanying concept. No claim that light travels rather than simply being present, no method of measurement, no derivation, no use made of the figure anywhere by anyone in the following six centuries. A number that can be made to match is not a discovery, and nobody in the tradition read it as one until the twentieth century.

items.claim: The Vedas state the law of gravitation.
items.html: The verse usually offered is Rigveda 10.149.1, which says that Savitṛ fastened the earth with bonds and made the sky firm in unsupported space. What this states is that a god holds the earth and sky in place — an image found in nearly every ancient cosmology from Mesopotamia to the Andes, and a beautiful one. What it does not contain is any of the things that make gravitation a law: no mass, no distance, no inverse-square relation, no universality, no prediction, no quantity. Reading it as Newton requires you to already know Newton and then go looking. And the irony is that Indian tradition does contain a genuine anticipation, which the people making this claim consistently overlook: in the Brāhmasphuṭasiddhānta of 628 CE, the astronomer Brahmagupta states that the earth attracts heavy bodies toward itself because attraction is the earth's nature — an actual physical proposition, made in an actual astronomical treatise. It is seventh-century mathematical astronomy, not Vedic hymnody, and it is more impressive than the fabrication.

items.claim: The Vedas give the age of the universe, and the yuga figures match modern cosmology.
items.html: It fails at the first step: the yuga chronology is not in the Vedas. The Rigveda Samhita contains no scheme of four ages with numerical durations. The developed system — Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara and Kali totalling 4,320,000 years to a mahāyuga, a thousand of which make a day of Brahmā — belongs to the epics, the law books, the Purāṇas and the later astronomical siddhāntas, composed one to two thousand years after the hymns. It then fails on the numbers: a day of Brahmā is 4.32 billion years; the universe is about 13.8 billion years old on Planck-mission microwave background data, and the Earth about 4.54 billion, the latter figure established by Clair Patterson's lead-isotope work in 1956. The near-agreement of 4.32 with 4.54 billion is regularly presented as a hit; it is a coincidence with no derivation behind it, drawn from a scheme that generates a great many numbers, and it is the wrong quantity in any case — a kalpa is a recurring cosmic day, not the age of a planet. Cyclical time is a magnificent idea and one of India's real contributions to how human beings have imagined the cosmos. It is not a measurement.

items.claim: The Vedas describe aircraft — the vimānas — and ancient Indians flew.
items.html: Three separate failures. First, the word. In the Rigveda, the root vi-mā means to measure out or traverse; there is no Vedic passage describing a flying machine. The flying palace called Puṣpaka belongs to the Rāmāyaṇa, and the vimāna as a celestial vehicle belongs to epic and Purāṇic literature — a thousand years and more after the hymns, and in a genre where gods also curse people into stones. Second, the text everyone actually means. The Vaimānika Śāstra, which contains the engineering-sounding descriptions and the famous diagrams, is not ancient. It was produced between about 1918 and 1923 by Pandit Subbaraya Shastry, who dictated it in a state he described as psychic reception from the sage Bharadvāja; it was written down by an assistant, surfaced publicly in the 1950s, and was published with an English translation in 1973. Third, it was checked. In 1974, five aeronautical engineers at the Indian Institute of Science in Bangalore — H. S. Mukunda, S. M. Deshpande, H. R. Nagendra, A. Prabhu and S. P. Govindaraju — published a critical study of the work. They analysed the described craft as engineering: geometry, dimensions, proposed propulsion, materials. Their conclusion was that the aircraft described are aeronautically hopeless, that none of the configurations could fly, that the drawings show twentieth-century influence, and that the text cannot be dated before the early 1900s. It is the rare pseudo-historical claim that has been given a genuine technical hearing by qualified people, and it failed on the merits.

blocks.html: The Pattern

Look back across those verdicts and notice the shape of the thing. Everything in the corroborated column concerns language, memory, ritual technique and the disciplines built around them — and in that territory the Vedic tradition's achievements are not merely real but, in the case of the transmission, without parallel anywhere on earth. Everything in the contradicted column concerns modern physics retrofitted into ancient verses, and every one of those readings collapses on inspection, usually within a paragraph.

That is not an accident, and it is worth saying why. The Vedic tradition was extraordinary at the things it was actually trying to do: preserving sound exactly, analysing speech, laying out altars, keeping a liturgy intact across millennia. It was not trying to do physics, and there is no reason it should have been. The claim that it secretly was is not a compliment to the tradition. It is a statement that the tradition's own priorities were not good enough, and that it needs a modern alibi to be worth respecting.
It does not. A civilisation that built a system for carrying ten thousand verses across three thousand years in human memory, and that produced Pāṇini, does not need to have known the speed of light.

blocks.tag: Practice · What to Do When You Meet the Claim

blocks.html: You will meet these claims. When you do, three questions dissolve nearly all of them, and none of them require you to be rude.

items: Which text, and which layer? Samhita, Brahmana, Upanishad, or a commentary written two thousand years later? An astonishing proportion of "Vedic" claims turn out to rest on Sāyaṇa, or on a Purāṇa, or on a twentieth-century book.
What does the verse say without the interpretation? Ask for the Sanskrit and a literal rendering. The gap between the verse and the claim is usually visible immediately.

Who used this knowledge, and when? If the speed of light was in the text, why did no Indian astronomer for six hundred years after Sāyaṇa ever mention it? Real knowledge in a living tradition gets used. Knowledge that appears only after the modern discovery is not knowledge; it is recognition.

blocks.html: At the beginning I asked you to write one sentence saying what you believed the Vedas contained. Find that page now, and read it before you read the rest of this.

I do not know what it says. Perhaps it was about ancient wisdom, or about mantras, or about something a grandparent said, or about a suspicion you did not want to admit to. Whatever it was, read it as though a stranger had written it, because in a small way one did — a person who had not yet met Indra, or the ghana-pāṭha, or a man in the tenth maṇḍala who cannot stop gambling.
What You Actually Have Now
Not very many facts. Facts are the first thing to go, and if in a year you remember that Maṇḍala 9 is about soma and that the Purusha Sukta is late, that is more than most people carry.

What may last is smaller and more useful. You now know that the Vedas are a library and not a book, and that the single most clarifying question you can ask about any Vedic claim is which layer. You know that the tradition's greatest achievement is a technique of memory, and you know exactly what that achievement does and does not prove. You know how to hold a text that is simultaneously a religious object, a historical document, and a work of poetry, without letting any one of those crush the others.

And you know something about honesty that has nothing to do with India. The habit we have practised here — say what the evidence shows, say clearly where it stops, do not sneer, do not inflate — is not a special method for handling scripture. It is just what it feels like to think carefully about something you care about. Most people never get to practise it on something they care about, which is why so few of them can do it.
The Fire and the Question
Two images to leave you with, and they are the two ends of this library.

The first is the first line of the Rigveda: a man before dawn, praising a fire. Not a philosopher. A person with cattle to protect and children who might not survive the winter, kindling a flame and speaking to it. Everything in the Indian religious tradition, all of it, comes out of that courtyard.

The second is what the same tradition had made of itself by the time it reached the tenth book — a poet who has walked all the way back to the beginning of things, past the gods, past being and non-being, and arrives at the edge, and stops, and does not lie about what he can see from there.

blocks.tag: Sanskrit · The Last Verse of the Creation Hymn
blocks.sk:
इयं विसृष्टिर्यत आबभूव यदि वा दधे यदि वा न ।
यो अस्याध्यक्षः परमे व्योमन्त्सो अङ्ग वेद यदि वा न वेद ॥
blocks.tr:
iyaṁ visṛṣṭir yata ābabhūva yadi vā dadhe yadi vā na |
yo asyādhyakṣaḥ parame vyoman so aṅga veda yadi vā na veda ||
blocks.mn: "Whence this creation came to be, whether it was established or whether it was not — he who watches over it from the highest heaven, he surely knows. Or perhaps he does not know."

blocks.html: so aṅga veda yadi vā na veda. He knows — or perhaps he does not know.

Three thousand years of the most careful preservation in human history were spent, among other things, on keeping that sentence exactly as it was. Not softened. Not completed. Not answered by a later hand. Every reciter who has carried the tenth maṇḍala since has come to the end of this hymn and said, out loud, in the correct pitch, that even the highest seer may not know.

That is what remains. Not a body of secret knowledge, and not a set of primitive errors — a very old voice, kept intact by an almost unreasonable effort, saying carefully and without shame that at the place where it stopped being able to see, it stopped.
The reading ends here. Oṁ śāntiḥ śāntiḥ śāntiḥ.
